## Summary

The inti was created in 1985 to replace a sol already worn down by inflation. Under price controls, a debt-service cap and deficits financed by the central bank, it went into hyperinflation twice: **114 % in September 1988**, then **397 % in August 1990** — the month of the stabilisation shock itself — with prices **doubling every 13.1 days** (H&K). In 1991 one nuevo sol replaced a million intis.

## Causes

- **The central bank financed the deficit** while tax receipts collapsed with inflation (the
  Olivera–Tanzi effect: taxes are paid in money that has lost value by the time it arrives).

## Timeline

- **1 Feb 1985** — the inti replaces the sol de oro at 1,000 : 1.
- **Sep 1988** — a devaluation package; prices rise 114 % in the month (H&K).
- **28 Jul 1990** — Alberto Fujimori takes office.
- **Aug 1990** — prices rise 397 % in the month (H&K).
- **1 Jul 1991** — the nuevo sol replaces the inti at 1 : 1,000,000.

## The end

The Fujishock was the textbook "pain first" exit: freed prices, a balanced cash budget (spend only what was collected), a floating exchange rate and a return to creditors. The nuevo sol has been one of Latin America's steadiest currencies since.

## Lessons

- Price controls hide inflation; they do not stop it. Lifting them produced the **worst single
  month** — the bill for every month they had hidden.
